Sports Betting Alliance Pushes Rhode Island to End Its Sportsbook Monopoly

Published November 15, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Sports Betting Alliance — the trade group representing DraftKings, FanDuel, Fanatics Sportsbook and BetMGM — is renewing its push to let more operators into Rhode Island's online sports betting market, releasing new data this week arguing the state's current single-platform setup is pushing bettors, and tax revenue, across the border. Alliance president and CEO Joe Maloney said in a statement that Rhode Islanders placed more than 4 million mobile bets in Massachusetts, Connecticut and New York over the past year — bets he argued could have stayed, and been taxed, in Rhode Island.

A one-operator market since legalization

Rhode Island has had only one licensed online sportsbook, SportsBook Rhode Island, since lawmakers legalized mobile betting in 2019 and handed the state's lottery regulators the authority to pick a single provider: IGT. That exclusive arrangement is set to expire later this month. Earlier in 2026, the Rhode Island Lottery Commission selected the state's sole land-based casino operator, Bally's, to run a second online platform — only one other company had bid for that contract — and a Bally's spokeswoman told local reporters this week that its app is targeting a December launch.

The numbers behind the pitch

The Alliance's figures, cited in reporting this week, put Rhode Island's online sports betting revenue at roughly $18 million over a recent one-year stretch, against roughly $170 million collected by Massachusetts over a comparable period — a state with about seven times Rhode Island's population but, by the Alliance's framing, nearly ten times its betting revenue. Massachusetts currently runs seven licensed online sportsbooks and taxes mobile betting revenue at 20%, well below the 51% share Rhode Island currently takes. The Alliance contends that opening Rhode Island to several more operators could add roughly $50 million in state revenue over the next decade.

A fight the legislature has already had once

This isn't a new argument in Providence. Representatives for DraftKings and FanDuel testified at the State House earlier in 2026 in support of a bill that would have allowed four to six licensed platforms; it passed the Rhode Island Senate but died in the House before the session ended. Rhode Island Lottery regulators opposed that expansion at the time, arguing a lower tax rate would be "financially detrimental" to the state and that Rhode Island's market is too small to support additional platforms beyond the two already in motion. FanDuel has separately said it chose not to bid on the state's second-operator contract because the state's revenue cut was too high. With the renewed push now aimed at the legislature again, the core disagreement — more operators and a lower tax rate versus a smaller number of platforms paying a bigger share to the state — looks largely unchanged from earlier this year.

Why it matters to bettors

For now, Rhode Island bettors still have just one live mobile option, with a second from Bally's expected within weeks. Nothing about this week's push changes that in the short term — any broader expansion would require new legislation to pass where a similar bill failed earlier this year. For bettors near state lines, the practical note is the one regulators always make: placing a mobile bet is legal only while physically located in a state where that platform is licensed, so a Rhode Island resident betting on a Massachusetts or Connecticut app needs to actually be in that state to do so legally.
